Where deeds and mortgages are recorded

Every deed, mortgage and judgment of possession for New Orleans property is recorded by the Land Records Division, part of the Orleans Parish Clerk of Civil District Court. It is at 1340 Poydras Street, 4th floor, New Orleans, LA 70112, phone (504) 407-0005.

The work used to be split among the Recorder of Mortgages, the Register of Conveyances and the Custodian of Notarial Archives. A 2006 consolidation law took effect January 1, 2009, and the clerk finished merging the three indexes into one system on February 18, 2014. Today there is one filing window. A cover sheet sorts the document into mortgage records, conveyance records or both.

  • Land Records Division: 1340 Poydras Street, 4th Floor, (504) 407-0005.
  • Research Center and historical records: 1340 Poydras Street, Suite 360, (504) 407-0106.
  • Civil Division (court filings): 421 Loyola Avenue, Room 402, (504) 407-0000.

Hours at all three: weekdays, 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM, with no lunch closing at Land Records. Legal holidays are listed on the clerk's hours page.

Recording fees and what is included

For a deed up to five pages, the base recording fee is $100. A $5 portal fee and a $30 building fund fee go on top. Call the office for the exact total before mailing a check.

La. R.S. 13:844 sets the base fee, which rises with page count. If one document goes into both the mortgage and conveyance records, you pay the fee twice. One certified copy and up to ten indexed names come with the base fee.

ChargeAmount
Recording, 1 to 5 pages$100
Recording, 6 to 25 pages$200
Recording, 26 to 50 pages$300
Each page over 50$5 added to $300
Louisiana Clerks' Remote Access Authority portal fee$5 per recording
Courthouse building fund fee$30 per recording
Each name indexed after the first ten$5
Survey, sketch or blueprint$30

Paperwork rules that get a deed rejected

Narrow margins can get a document rejected or hit with a $20 surcharge, since pages are bound into record books. Leave two inches at the top of page one and one inch at the bottom and both sides of every page. Type can be no smaller than eight point, and page one needs a caption saying what kind of act it is.

  • Odd paper sizes (anything but 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches) add $20 per page.
  • Attached surveys, tax certificates and mortgage certificates are counted in the page total.
  • Plan on not getting the original back, because recorded documents are bound into books.

How to pay: by mail, a business check or money order made out to Clerk of Court (personal checks are refused). At the counter, cash and major credit cards also work. eRecording runs through CSC, ePN and Simplifile, but cancellations, certificates, surveys and a few other document types cannot be filed that way.

New Orleans documentary transaction tax

New Orleans taxes documents that transfer or create property rights in the parish. The Notarial Archives collects for the city, and the taxed documents include sales, donations, transfers, mortgages and commercial leases.

The flat amount is $325 per taxable document. Mortgages with a loan amount under $9,000 use a smaller scale: $75 under $3,000, $125 from $3,000.01 to $6,000, and $175 from $6,000.01 to $9,000.

  • The seller, donor, mortgagor or commercial lessee is responsible.
  • Payment comes at recording, or after a bill within 30 days.
  • Late payment adds interest and a $500 penalty.
  • A taxable document other than a single-family home or residential double that runs over 25 pages adds $100 per page, up to $2,525.
  • A single-family home or residential double stays at $325 past 25 pages if a notarized statement says the owner lives there.

When a sale is eRecorded, the tax goes by check or money order to the City of New Orleans, with the recordation information on it. The clerk's documentary tax page has the rest. You are the responsible party as seller, so find this line on your closing statement.

Searching Orleans Parish land records

You can search at no cost on the clerk's public computers on the 3rd, 4th and 5th floors of 1340 Poydras Street, or remotely with a paid subscription. Searchable fields: name, municipal address, filing date, document type, and legal description by District, Square and Lot.

  • Mortgage index: September 21, 1987 through February 14, 2014.
  • Conveyance index: January 1, 1989 through February 14, 2014.
  • Unified Indexing System: February 18, 2014 forward.
  • Document images: January 1, 2005 forward, with some from 1970 to 2004.

Online Records subscriptions cost $20 for 24 hours, $100 for a month or $700 for a year, and downloading or printing images needs a separate escrow account. The state portal eClerks LA is free and searches indexes for all 64 parishes at once. A copy is $1 per page, with ID required only for a military discharge.

Clearing liens and mortgages before a sale

A mortgage you have paid off stays on the record until the lender's release paperwork is delivered to Land Records. Recording the cancellation costs $50, a Certificate of Cancellation adds $13, and the request cannot be filed electronically.

Title companies commonly order a mortgage certificate ahead of closing. The price is $20 for the first name and $10 per extra name. A conveyance certificate runs $35 for the first name and $30 for each additional one. A mortgage certificate shows lien information for up to 30 years.

Contractor liens follow a clock. Nobody can request a lien and privilege certificate until an Acceptance, Substantial Completion or Termination is recorded and the lien period has run: 30 days at least, longer if the contract says. If repair work was recently done on your house, check for this before you list.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Orleans Parish houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What Louisiana calls a deed

Title moves by an Act of Sale, which the clerk says can be styled a Cash Sale, a Credit Sale or a Warranty Deed. Louisiana follows civil law, so none of this matches the grant and quitclaim deeds of other states.

Civil Code art. 1839 says real property passes by authentic act or by act under private signature, and that outsiders are bound only once it is filed for registry in the parish where the land lies. That is why the Orleans filing matters. La. R.S. 9:2721 adds that the deed must say who answers for property taxes and give a mailing address for tax notices. Judgments of possession are recorded in the same division as sales and mortgages.

Recording a cash sale

Even a cash purchase finishes at Land Records, with the same paperwork whoever the buyer is. Staff can explain the filing steps, but they cannot give legal advice or choose documents for you.

  • Ask the closing office whether the deed will be eRecorded or hand delivered.
  • Ask who is paying the $325 documentary tax and where it shows on the settlement statement.
  • Order a mortgage certificate early so open liens surface well before closing day.
  • Confirm that recorded cancellations were actually filed, using the mortgage instrument number and the Cancel Status field. A C means fully cancelled and a P means partly cancelled.

Inherited houses, missed payments and homes needing repairs are common reasons owners look at a cash sale, and the recording steps above stay the same for each.

Frequently asked questions

Where is the Orleans Parish clerk of court's land records office?

The Land Records Division is at 1340 Poydras Street, 4th floor, New Orleans, LA 70112. It is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM and stays open at lunch. The phone number is (504) 407-0005.

How much is the recording fee for a deed in Orleans Parish?

The base fee is $100 for one to five pages, $200 for six to 25 pages and $300 for 26 to 50 pages, plus $5 for each page over 50. A $5 portal fee and a $30 building fund fee are added to each recording.

Is there a transfer tax when you sell a house in New Orleans?

The city charges a documentary transaction tax of $325 on a sale, and the seller is responsible for it. It is paid at recording or billed and due within 30 days, after which interest and a $500 penalty apply. It is separate from the recording fee.

Can I record a deed by mail or online in Orleans Parish?

Yes to both. Mail the original with a business check or money order payable to Clerk of Court, or use an eRecording vendor such as CSC, ePN or Simplifile. Personal checks and fax filings are not accepted for deeds.

How do I remove a paid-off mortgage from the record in Orleans Parish?

Bring the lender's release paperwork to the Land Records Division at 1340 Poydras Street. Cancelling a single mortgage costs $50, and an optional Certificate of Cancellation costs $13 more. Cancellations cannot be submitted by eRecording.

Clerk of Court offices and hours

The Terrebonne Parish Clerk of Court main office is at 7856 Main Street in Houma, and it keeps the conveyance and mortgage records for the parish. It is open 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Monday through Friday, and the main phone is 985-868-5660. The mailing address is PO Box 1569, Houma, LA 70361-1569.

Some services are in other buildings, so check before you drive.

ServiceLocation
Main office, recording7856 Main Street, Houma
Birth, death and marriage records, appeals310 Church Street, Houma
Elections, jury, passports by appointment415 Goode Street, Houma

Conveyance, mortgage, recording, indexing and maps are separate departments, so a deed passes through several hands.

How to record a deed

You record a deed by filing the notarized act of sale with the clerk, either in person or through e-recording on ClerkConnect. Louisiana requires the transfer to be made by authentic act or act under private signature, and it binds third persons only once filed in the conveyance records of the parish where the house stands.

The closing notary or title company usually files for you. Still, the act has to be right:

  • name the buyer and seller as they appear in the earlier title;
  • include a legal description of the property;
  • designate the person responsible for property taxes and an address for notices, as La. R.S. 9:2721 requires.

Anyone who acquires immovable property that is subject to a lease recorded earlier takes the property subject to that lease. If you have a recorded lease, tell the buyer.

Recording fees

Recording starts at $105 for one to five pages in one index type. Documents of 6 to 25 pages are $205, and 26 to 50 pages are $305, each per recording book.

Because the schedule counts pages, a short deed costs less to file than a long package. Ask whether exhibits or a legal description attachment change the page count. Call the clerk to confirm the current fee before you send a check, and ask your notary or title company what applies to your closing.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Terrebonne Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

From signing to public record: the timeline

It helps to picture the whole path of a Terrebonne sale, because the clerk's office is only one stop on it.

  1. The seller and buyer agree on terms, and a title company or notary opens the file.
  2. The title work starts with a search of the land records for the last recorded transfer, any mortgage and any lien.
  3. A mortgage certificate from the clerk's mortgage department shows what is recorded against the house.
  4. Any mortgage is paid off from the proceeds, and a cancellation is recorded so the record is clean.
  5. The notary prepares the act of sale with the legal description and the tax designation, and buyer and seller sign it.
  6. The act is filed with the clerk, in person or by e-recording, and the recording fee is paid from closing funds.

Until step six is done, the sale does not bind outsiders. That is why closing agents file the same day when they can.

A cash buyer shortens steps one and two, since no lender is waiting on an appraisal. Steps three through six look the same for every buyer.

What to bring and what to ask

If you go to the main office yourself, or send someone, bring the documents that show how you came to own the house: your deed, any succession papers and the payoff letter for any loan. A legal description copied from your last deed saves time.

Ask the staff three things. First, what the current recording fee is for the number of pages you have. Second, whether the act can go through e-recording on ClerkConnect or has to be filed in person. Third, which department handles any cancellation you need.

You can also pick up the answer to a different question while you are there. The clerk's civil records sit alongside the land records, so a person untangling an estate can check both in one trip. Services such as birth, death and marriage records are at the Church Street office, not the Main Street office, so do not go to the wrong building.

Searching land records online

You can search for free through the Louisiana Clerks of Court portal at eclerksla.com, and the Terrebonne clerk also runs its own eSearch. The free statewide search covers land, civil, criminal and marriage records from participating parishes.

The clerk's eSearch account page mentions a $10.00 fee for some uses and accepts prepayments from $1 to $1,000. Search before you list, looking for old mortgages, liens or an earlier sale that was never cleared.

The clerk also promotes eClerks Alerts, a free service that notifies you when a document bearing your registered name is recorded in any parish. Owners of a vacant or inherited house may find it useful, because it can flag a fraudulent filing.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Terrebonne Parish houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Storms, flooding and what buyers ask

Terrebonne is a Gulf Coast parish, with Houma as the seat and largest city. Hurricane Ida struck Houma as a Category 4 storm on August 29, 2021, and Hurricane Francine made landfall in the parish on September 11, 2024. Storm damage, roof repairs and insurance claims are common themes in local house sales, and a buyer will ask for proof of past repairs. Keep invoices and claim paperwork together.

Bayou lots add another wrinkle. The legal description of a bayou-side lot can be longer or more complicated than a subdivision lot in town, and surveys, servitudes and old family transfers sometimes appear in the chain of title.

Inherited and family-held houses

A house passed through a death often needs a succession handled first. The clerk keeps both the civil records and the land records, so one office holds the whole trail. Once the succession is done, the heirs sign the act of sale like any other owner.

If the succession was never opened, expect extra time and cost, and plan for that before you set a closing date.

  • Search the land records for the last recorded transfer into the family.
  • Check the civil records for an open or closed succession.
  • Find out whether any heir lives out of state and needs to sign remotely.

The statewide eClerks search helps relatives elsewhere in Louisiana see what is recorded without a trip to Houma.

What to check before closing

Before closing, confirm that the title is clean, the taxes are current and the act of sale matches the recorded chain of title. A mortgage certificate shows liens, and the clerk's mortgage department issues them.

  • Get a payoff for any mortgage and confirm how it will be cancelled in the records.
  • Ask the parish tax collector for a tax payoff at 985-857-0230.
  • Check for a succession if an owner has died, since a deed needs someone with authority to sign.
  • Confirm whether a recorded lease binds the buyer.

For a cash sale, the same filings apply. The buyer or the title company can e-record the day of closing, so ownership shows up in the public record quickly.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Terrebonne Parish?

You record it with the Terrebonne Parish Clerk of Court at 7856 Main Street, Houma, or through e-recording on ClerkConnect.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Terrebonne Parish?

The schedule lists $105 for one to five pages, $205 for 6 to 25 and $305 for 26 to 50. Confirm the current fee with the office before you pay.

Is there a transfer tax in Terrebonne Parish?

Ask the clerk or your closing notary to confirm the total for your sale. Recording fees are set by page count.

Can I search Terrebonne property records for free?

Yes. The Louisiana Clerks of Court portal offers a free statewide search of land, civil, criminal and marriage records.

What must a Louisiana deed say about taxes?

It must name the person responsible for property taxes and give an address for tax notices, under La. R.S. 9:2721.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Jefferson Parish?

Jefferson Parish clerk of court: what it is

Louisiana has parishes instead of counties, so anyone searching for the Jefferson County clerk of court is looking for the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court, based in Gretna. Its Mortgage and Conveyance department keeps the parish's official land records, which is where a house sale ends up on paper. The Clerk also runs records for the 24th Judicial District Court, the First and Second Parish Courts and the Juvenile Court.

Jefferson is a large suburban parish next to New Orleans, split by the Mississippi River into an East Bank and a West Bank. The 2020 census counted 440,781 residents. Gretna is the parish seat, Metairie is the largest community and Kenner is the largest incorporated city. The land records office sits on the West Bank, so a seller in Metairie or Kenner who wants to look at records in person has to cross the river. Most people skip the drive and let the closing agent file electronically, as described below.

Where to record a deed

Deeds and other real estate documents go to the Mortgage and Conveyance/UCC department in the Jefferson Parish General Government Building, 200 Derbigny Street, Suite 2200, Gretna, LA 70053. The office is open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, closed on legal holidays. The mailing address is P.O. Box 10, Gretna, LA 70054-0010.

  • Prices and copies: (504) 364-2943 or (504) 364-2944.
  • Certificates and UCC research: (504) 364-2954.
  • Mortgage cancellations: (504) 364-2963.
  • Email: mortgageinfo@jeffparishclerk.gov.

This office records real estate transfers and acts of sale, mortgages, liens and judgments, military discharges, corporation charters, trade name affidavits, and oil, gas and mineral lease transfers. The East Bank office in the Joseph S. Yenni Building handles marriage licenses, passports and elections. Take land records to Gretna.

How soon must an act of sale be recorded?

A notary has 15 days to record a sale of land outside Orleans Parish. R.S. 35:199 requires notaries to file acts of sale, exchange, donation and mortgage of immovable property with the proper parish recorder within fifteen days.

Here is how it plays out. You sign the act of sale before a notary at closing. The title company or closing attorney then sends the act to the Clerk. Because the duty falls on the notary, the closing agent normally handles the filing. Your job is to supply a correct legal description and sign where asked.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Jefferson Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Recording fees

Recording a document of 1 to 5 pages costs $105 at the Jefferson Parish Clerk. Mortgage and conveyance fees are set by the Legislature under R.S. 13:844, and the office receives no ad valorem tax funding, so fees pay for its operations.

Document lengthRecording fee
1 to 5 pages$105.00
6 to 25 pages$205.00
26 to 50 pages$305.00
51 pages or more$305.00 for the first 50 pages, then $5.00 per page

The base fee covers every part of the act and its attachments: exhibits, powers of attorney, property descriptions, tax certificates and surveys. It includes one certified copy and indexing of up to ten names. Extra names cost $5.00 each, pages larger than 8.5 by 14 inches add $20.00 per page, and the fee is charged once per book designation, so a document recorded as both a conveyance and a mortgage costs double.

Every recording since August 1, 2018 also carries a $5.00 fee under R.S. 13:754 that supports the statewide LCRAA system, charged once per instrument.

Is there a transfer tax on a Jefferson Parish sale?

The Clerk's fee schedule has no transfer tax line. A sale involves the recording charge, any certificates ordered and the optional extras closing agents add. Your closing attorney or title company prepares the settlement statement, so ask them what applies to your deal.

Other charges you may see on the Clerk's schedule:

  • Mortgage or lien and privilege certificate: $20.00 for the first name and $10.00 for each additional name, plus $40.00 if clerk staff prepare it.
  • Act or affidavit to cancel a single mortgage, lien or privilege: $55.00.
  • Release of a mortgage with the original paraphed note: $10.00 per mortgage. A Notice of Cancellation adds $10.00 per mortgage inscription released.
  • Copies: $1.00 per page uncertified, and $10.00 per document certified plus copy costs for mortgage records.

Since April 7, 2017, Jefferson Certificate Corp. in Gretna has prepared mortgage and conveyance certificates under contract with the Clerk. Call (504) 361-0206 for ordinary acts of sale or mortgage.

Recording online with JeffNet

Yes, a Jefferson Parish deed can be recorded online. The Clerk takes mortgage and conveyance documents, including requests to cancel mortgage inscriptions, through JeffNet, its secure online records system. It gives 24-hour access to property, civil, criminal and other public records.

  • 24-hour access: $5.00. Certified copies run $0.75 per page plus a $10.00 certification fee for mortgage records.
  • Monthly subscription: $50.00 per user ID. It covers e-filing and e-recording, and every monthly subscriber can use it, not only attorneys.

With e-recording, your closing agent can file the sale without a trip to Gretna. You can buy the 24-hour option yourself to look up the recorded mortgage on your house before you list.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Jefferson Parish houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Estate and foreclosure filings

Two court filings come up often for sellers who cannot close cleanly. One is a succession, the court process for settling a deceased owner's estate, which is how an inherited house in Gretna, Marrero, Kenner or elsewhere in the parish gets cleared for sale. The other is executory process, Louisiana's foreclosure suit. The civil fee table lists advance deposits for both, and treats them as a guide, since the actual charge can vary.

  • Succession under $125,000 (La. C.C.P. Art. 3422): $200.00 deposit.
  • Succession of $125,000 and over: $400.00 deposit.
  • Executory process (foreclosure): $1,000.00 deposit.
  • Judicial eviction trial in a Parish Court: $375.00 plus a bond set by the court.

The 24th JDC civil records are at 200 Derbigny Street, Suite 2400, in the same complex as the land records office, so one trip can cover both.

Seller checklist for closing day

Before the act of sale is signed, check three things. Confirm the legal description on your documents is correct, because the Clerk indexes and records exactly what is filed. Find out whether an old mortgage is still recorded against the house. If one is, the lender's release has to be filed, and a cancellation costs $55.00 or the lower release fees listed above. Then ask the title company whether they will e-record, which spares everyone a trip across the river.

If the house came to you through an estate, ask the closing attorney whether the succession is finished. The court filing has to be done before a buyer's title company will clear the sale. A cash buyer can close faster than most in these cases, since there is no lender waiting on its own paperwork.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Jefferson Parish?

The Mortgage and Conveyance/UCC department of the Jefferson Parish Clerk of Court records deeds at 200 Derbigny Street, Suite 2200, Gretna, LA 70053. It is open weekdays from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Jefferson Parish?

The fee is $105.00 for 1 to 5 pages, $205.00 for 6 to 25 pages and $305.00 for 26 to 50 pages, plus $5.00 per page beyond 50. A $5.00 LCRAA fee also applies to each recording.

Does Jefferson Parish charge a transfer tax on a sale?

The Clerk's fee schedule has no transfer tax line. Ask your closing attorney or title company what will appear on your settlement statement.

Can my title company e-record a Jefferson Parish deed?

Yes, through JeffNet. E-recording comes with a monthly subscription at $50.00 per user ID, and any subscriber can use it, not only attorneys.

How long does a notary have to record a sale in Jefferson Parish?

Fifteen days. R.S. 35:199 requires notaries to file sales of immovable property outside Orleans Parish with the parish recorder within fifteen days after the act is passed.

What the clerk does with your deed

The clerk records the deed, and that filing is what makes a Louisiana sale effective against everyone outside the contract. Under Civil Code article 3338, a written transfer of land has no effect on third persons until it is recorded in the conveyance records.

The Lafayette Parish clerk serves the 15th Judicial District and acts as ex-officio recorder. The Recording Department files conveyance, mortgage and UCC documents. Each document gets an entry number with the date, hour and minute of filing, and a short description with the first parties shows up on the online records search right away. Between two and three hundred documents come in daily, and full indexing of all party names is done by the next day.

Office: 800 S. Buchanan St., Lafayette, LA 70501. Mail: P.O. Box 2009, Lafayette, LA 70502. Main number (337) 291-6400, Recording Department (337) 291-6310.

Recording fees

A conveyance or mortgage of one to five pages costs $105 to record in a single index type. Every price below already includes the $5 statewide portal fee, indexing of up to ten names and one certified copy.

Document lengthOne book (conveyance or mortgage)Both books
1 to 5 pages$105$205
6 to 25 pages$205$405
26 to 50 pages$305$605
51 pages or more$305 plus $5 per extra page$605 plus $5 per extra page

Use the two-book column when a single document goes into both records. Fees are charged for each book, except that the $5 portal charge applies once. Extras: $5 for each name after the tenth, $20 per page for paper other than 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches, and $25 per debtor on a judgment with no Social Security or tax ID number.

A new recording charge starts in 2027

Act 446 of the 2026 Regular Legislative Session adds $5 to every recorded document, effective January 1, 2027. A closing in late December 2026 and one in early January 2027 can therefore show different recording totals.

The existing $5 portal fee comes from Act 173 of 2017 and took effect August 1, 2018. It pays for the Louisiana Clerks Remote Access Authority, a state entity that runs a statewide portal for remote access to parish land records. Both charges are on top of the page-based fee, so get the total from the closing office before closing day.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Lafayette Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Other charges at closing

Smaller line items appear around the main recording fee:

  • Cancellation or partial release of a single mortgage, lien or privilege: $55.
  • Cancellation with the original paraphed note: $15.
  • Real estate mortgage certificate: $20 for the first name, $10 for each additional name, and $15 for each additional property.
  • Non-lien certificate: $20 per name.
  • Copies: $1 per page in the office, $10 plus the copy fee for a certified copy, and $5 plus the copy fee for a conformed copy.

A mortgage certificate lists the recorded mortgages and privileges against a seller's name. Title agents order one so every lien is confirmed paid and cancelled before the buyer's money is released. The fee schedule has no transfer tax line, so ask your closing agent for the full settlement figures.

How to prepare and submit documents

Each document needs a caption on its first page naming the type of act. Leave a 2 inch margin at the top and 1 inch at the bottom and sides, and use type no smaller than 8 point. Paper can be 8.5 by 11 or 8.5 by 14 inches. These rules come from R.S. 13:844(B).

All pages presented together count as one document, including exhibits, riders, powers of attorney, property descriptions, tax certificates, surveys and mortgage certificates. The count sets the price tier.

The clerk prefers electronic recording and links three e-recording platforms from its home page: CSC, ePN and Simplifile. Most title companies already use one. If you mail a paper act, enclose a self-addressed stamped envelope or pay postage at actual cost.

Original documents are not returned

Unlike in most states, originals sent to the Clerk of the District Court and Ex-Officio Recorder stay in the parish archives. You can get a certified copy instead, either when you file, from the Recording Department, or later, from the Land Records and Copy Department. Order that copy during closing if the Assessor or a lender will want proof of the sale.

Cancellations take a separate route. They go first to the Cancellation Clerk in the Recording Department for verification, and in Lafayette Parish they must be in authentic form, signed by the affiant before a notary public. UCC terminations use a Louisiana-approved form and can be sent directly.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Lafayette Parish houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Searching Lafayette Parish land records

The clerk's online search covers mortgage, conveyance and UCC records. The free eClerks LA portal indexes land, civil, marriage and probate records across Louisiana, and a free alert service there watches land records in other parishes.

Paid access with document images is sold by subscription: $20 for one day, $50 for 30 days or $600 for 365 days, plus $1 per page to print. Searching liens under your name before you list can turn up a forgotten mortgage or judgment that would otherwise surface at closing.

Filings may become public record under the Public Records Act. The courthouse bars cellphones, cameras and recording devices, so bring paper documents and a printed list of the numbers you need.

From signing to recorded

Here is the usual path for a Lafayette Parish sale. You sign the act of sale at closing. The title company or closing attorney submits it, ideally through one of the e-recording platforms. The Recording Department stamps it with the entry number, date, hour and minute, and the online search shows a short description soon after. Full indexing is done the next day.

If an old mortgage is being paid off, its cancellation travels the same road, through the Cancellation Clerk first. Once the act is recorded, ask for the certified copy. Keep it with your closing papers, since originals are not returned.

Checklist before the deed is recorded

Louisiana lets any party to a conveyance of real property outside New Orleans get a certificate showing whether state, parish, municipal and levee district taxes are paid, other than those for the year of the sale (R.S. 9:2901).

  • Ask for the tax certificate and for a mortgage certificate on every owner's name.
  • Make sure any prior mortgage has a cancellation ready to record.
  • Ask the closing office whether the recording date falls before or after January 1, 2027.
  • Request a certified copy of the recorded act for your own file.

A seller taking a cash offer should run the same list, since the buyer's title agent will do these searches before funding. Problems are cheaper to fix before closing day.

Frequently asked questions

How much does it cost to record a deed in Lafayette Parish?

A one to five page conveyance in a single book costs $105, which includes a $5 portal fee, ten indexed names and one certified copy. Six to 25 pages costs $205.

Is there a transfer tax on the Lafayette Parish fee schedule?

The schedule lists recording, cancellation, copy and certificate fees but no transfer tax line. Ask your closing agent for the full settlement figures.

Does the Lafayette Parish clerk return my original deed?

No. Originals become part of the parish archives. You can get a certified copy at filing or later from the Land Records and Copy Department.

Can I e-record a deed in Lafayette Parish?

Yes, and the clerk encourages it. The clerk's site links to CSC, ePN and Simplifile for electronic recording of mortgage, conveyance and UCC documents.

What changes on January 1, 2027?

Act 446 of the 2026 Regular Legislative Session adds $5 to every recorded document starting that date.

Cash Home Buyers in Louisiana
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

Last updated November 14, 2026.

What the clerk does when a house sells

In Louisiana's parishes (what other states call counties), the clerk doubles as parish recorder. Deeds, mortgages and other property papers become public record at the recording desk, which is the office buyers, sellers, title companies and heirs all end up dealing with.

A deputy clerk stamps each incoming document with a unique instrument number plus an index book and page number, and the stamp records the date, hour and minute of filing.

Under Civil Code article 3346, an instrument creating or relating to a mortgage or privilege on land goes into the parish mortgage records. Every other instrument, an act of sale included, goes into the conveyance records. One closing in Livingston Parish can therefore put papers into both sets of books.

Office location and hours

The main office is at 20300 Government Blvd., Livingston, LA 70754, mailing address P. O. Box 1150. Call 225-686-2216 or fax 225-686-1867. A satellite office in Denham Springs sits at 145 Del Orleans Avenue, Bldg. 2, Suite E, 70726. Phone ahead to confirm it takes recordings.

Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. The office closes on legal holidays, so plan any closing near these remaining 2026 dates around them:

  • Thursday and Friday, November 26 and 27 (Thanksgiving and the day after)
  • Thursday, December 24, Friday, December 25 and Thursday, December 31

Recording fees

A deed or mortgage of one to five pages costs $125 to record. Longer documents cost more, and a few extras apply to indexing and to badly formatted papers.

ServiceFee
Recording, pages 1 to 5$125.00
Recording, pages 6 to 25$225.00
Recording, pages 26 to 50$325.00
Indexing, first ten names per bookIncluded
Each additional name per book$5
Copies, per page$1.00
Certified copy$10.00
Conformed copy$5.00
Cancellation of mortgage, original note$35.00
Cancellation with affidavit$75.00

Schedules can change, so ask the office for the current total before closing. Your title company or closing attorney normally submits the deed, so ask them to confirm the page count, the number of names and whether both mortgage and conveyance books are involved.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Livingston Parish house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Transfer tax

The fee schedule covers recording, indexing, copy, map and cancellation charges. It has no per-dollar transfer tax. What the clerk collects pays for handling pages and names, not a percentage of your price. Mortgage payoff and unpaid property tax are settled between the parties and the title company.

Deed format rules

Louisiana statutes set the format, and a document that misses it can draw an extra $10 noncompliance fee. Under R.S. 13:844(D)(1), the first page must be captioned by type of act, with a two inch margin at the top, one inch at the bottom and sides, and type no smaller than eight point. Multiple indebtedness mortgages follow the same rule under R.S. 9:5217(B).

  • Caption the first page with the type of act.
  • Leave the margins described above.
  • Use type of eight point or larger.
  • Do not expect the original back. Originals are not returned and become part of the parish archives.

For proof of what you filed, ask at filing for a certified copy with the clerk's endorsement.

Mortgage certificates and cancellations

The mortgage section issues certificates and cancels mortgage inscriptions, and both begin with a written request. Louisiana law requires certificate requests in writing, and the office takes them by fax too. Name the exact people to check and give a legal property description.

A mortgage certificate, properly called a certificate of non-mortgage, is not a title opinion and says nothing about who owns the property. It lists what is recorded against the names searched.

Since July 1, 2006, a borrower who pays off a mortgage on Livingston Parish real estate is responsible for seeing that the mortgage is cancelled. The office needs the original note marked "paid" on its face and will not take faxes or copies. If the note is lost, go back to the lender. Lost note affidavits have mostly given way, under R.S. 44:109, to an authentic act from a financial institution.

A mortgage paid years ago but never cancelled can surface late in a sale. Check the mortgage records early so there is time to fix it.

Researching a property's records

The conveyance section lets the public research property transactions, mineral leases, restrictions and subdivision maps through written or computerized indexes dating back to 1875. Large-screen computer stations serve real estate agents, surveyors, appraisers, abstractors and attorneys, and staff help is free.

Surveys cause trouble. Louisiana law does not require a survey of conveyed property to be recorded or separately indexed, so some were never recorded or cannot be found. The mapping section keeps a map index showing for whom a map was prepared, the property size, its location and the surveyor, and a surveyor may hold a copy the clerk lacks.

For ownership lines, use the parish ownership map on livingstonassessor.com.

Livingston Parish and the 2016 flood

Livingston Parish lies east of Baton Rouge. Denham Springs, Walker, Livingston, Albany and Springfield are its towns and cities, and the main clerk's office is in the town of Livingston, the parish seat. It is one of the fastest-growing parishes in the state, with Interstate 12 as its east-west route.

The August 2016 flood still comes up in nearly every house conversation. A state economic impact report estimated that 38,300 of the parish's 52,104 housing units flooded. The Amite River gauge at Denham Springs lists August 14, 2016 as the flood of record. Sellers will see it in three ways:

  • Buyers and lenders ask whether the house took water, what was rebuilt and who did the work.
  • Elevation, flood zone and insurance history become part of price talks.
  • Repair records, permits and contractor payments help answer those questions.

A flood-history house that still needs work is a common reason owners consider an as-is sale over repairing and listing.

Heirs and owners with a distressed house

Start with the recorded history. Pull the conveyance records for the last transfer, then the mortgage records for open liens. A clean record of who owns the house and what is owed makes any sale, cash or otherwise, move faster.

If the owner died, the paperwork that moves title to heirs is a court or affidavit process described in our Louisiana estate tax guide, and it ends with a document that goes to the same recording desk. For rentals, see our guides on the eviction process and the eviction notice.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Livingston Parish?

At the Livingston Parish Clerk of Court's recording desk, 20300 Government Blvd., Livingston, LA 70754. A Denham Springs satellite office exists, but phone first to confirm it takes recordings. The main number is 225-686-2216.

How much is the recording fee for a short deed in Livingston Parish?

It is $125 for pages 1 to 5, $225 for pages 6 to 25 and $325 for pages 26 to 50, with the first ten names per book included in indexing. Check with the office for the current total.

Does the Livingston Parish clerk return the original deed?

No. Originals become part of the parish archives. You can request a certified copy with the clerk's endorsement at filing.

Who cancels a paid-off mortgage in Livingston Parish?

The borrower is responsible. Since July 1, 2006, the borrower, not the lender, bears the risk if a paid mortgage is never cancelled, and the office needs the original note marked paid.

Can I sell a flood-damaged Livingston Parish house as-is?

Yes, but expect buyers to ask for repair, permit and insurance history. Get your recorded title and mortgage payoff in order first so the record does not slow the sale.

What the clerk does in a home sale

The Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court keeps the parish's public land records, so a deed, mortgage or mortgage cancellation for a Monroe or West Monroe house gets filed there. After you sign, your closing attorney or title company deals with the recording department.

The office also handles civil and criminal filings, marriage licenses, birth and death certificate requests, assumed name certificates and passport applications. A seller only needs the recording department. The office phone is (318) 327-1444, and the courthouse is on South Grand Street in Monroe.

Ouachita Parish covers 632 square miles, with Monroe as its seat and largest city. The clerk in Monroe keeps records for the whole parish, so a house in West Monroe, Richwood, Sterlington, Calhoun or Swartz is recorded in the same place.

Hours and payment

The office is open Monday through Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., except legal holidays. Closures include Thanksgiving Day, the Friday after Thanksgiving, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and New Year's Eve in 2026. If your closing falls near one of those dates, ask your title company how recording will be timed.

The office accepts no personal checks. Online accounts and copies are paid by credit card (Visa, MasterCard, Discover or American Express). A third-party convenience fee of 3.49 percent applies, with a $1.00 minimum, under La. R.S. 13:841 and Act No. 403.

  • Hours: Monday to Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.
  • Phone: (318) 327-1444.
  • Personal checks: not accepted.
  • Cards: accepted online with a 3.49 percent fee, $1.00 minimum.

Searching land records online

You search Ouachita Parish land records through a Clerk Connect account, which is a paid subscription covering civil inquiry, criminal inquiry and property records. Certified copies can be ordered online too.

Access optionPrice
Day rate (24 hours)$20.00

The clerk also promotes a free "eClerks Alert" service that watches land and criminal records across Louisiana parishes. The online system is at opclerkofcourt.com, and account help is available by phone at extension 3501.

A quick search of your own parcel before you list can show an old mortgage or lien you forgot about. Gather the parcel number, last deed and any survey at the same time, and the closing moves faster.

How a deed gets recorded

A deed is recorded by presenting the signed act of sale to the recording department, in person or through the clerk's electronic filing system. Most sellers never do this. The closing attorney or notary files the sale and the mortgage cancellation after signing.

Electronic filing has technical standards. Submissions must be PDF files of at least 300 DPI, with plain file names of 50 characters or fewer, no password protection and no embedded video, audio or other PDFs.

Under Act No. 352 of the 2025 Regular Session, now part of Code of Civil Procedure Article 253(B)(2) and (3), attorney filings can no longer be faxed or mailed. They must be filed in person on paper or sent electronically through a clerk's system or the Louisiana Clerks' Remote Access Authority.

Ask the recording department or your closing attorney for the cost before closing day.

Transfer tax and your settlement statement

The closing statement your title company prepares shows every recording charge and any tax that applies to your sale.

Ask for a draft several days before closing. It should list recording fees, the mortgage cancellation fee, prorated property tax and any payoff to the Sheriff's Tax Office. Comparing that draft with the clerk's fee information is the simplest way to catch an error.

Liens and tax items in the record

The land records show mortgages, recorded liens and the assessment roll lien that attaches to a property for unpaid property tax. Under La. R.S. 47:1993, once the assessor's roll is delivered to the recorder of mortgages, it acts as a lien and privilege on each property assessed.

That lien generally ranks ahead of other encumbrances, apart from prior-year rolls and tax lien certificates. A buyer's title examiner will look for exactly these items. If one turns up, the seller usually has to pay it off or arrange for it to be paid at closing.

The Ouachita Parish Sheriff collects the tax as ex-officio tax collector, and the Tax Office number is 318-324-2536. Late taxes accrue 1 percent interest per month, and a tax sale carries a three-year right of redemption for immovable property.

Sheriff sales and foreclosures

Court-ordered seizures go through the Sheriff's Civil Division, and the sales are posted publicly. The division handles writs of seizure and sale, garnishments, attachments and writs of possession. After advertising in the legal section of a local newspaper, property is sold at public auction.

Sales are held every Wednesday morning at 10:00 a.m. through an online bidding site. The same office serves civil papers and carries out evictions on seized and sold property when occupants do not leave as directed.

The Sheriff acts on orders from the parish courts and the 4th Judicial District Court. If your house is in or near foreclosure, the recorded seizure and the court record both limit what a buyer can do, so talk to an attorney about timing.

Timeline from signing to recorded

Here is what the path looks like. You sign the act of sale before the notary at closing. The closing attorney or title company then sends the act to the recording department, usually electronically, as a PDF that meets the clerk's standards. The mortgage cancellation for any loan being paid off is filed along with it. After that, the sale shows up in the land records, and a new owner can be found by anyone who searches the parcel.

If something is rejected, the filing agent fixes the document and sends it again, which is one more reason to ask the title company early how long recording usually takes. Keep your copy of the settlement statement. It lists each recording charge, so you can match it against what the clerk actually charged.

Before you list: a short checklist

A few steps save trouble on closing day. Pull your parcel's record and read the last deed, so the legal description in the new act of sale matches. Ask the Sheriff's Tax Office for the amount owed on your property tax and confirm it is current. Make sure any paid-off mortgage has been cancelled of record. Then give your closing attorney or title company the survey, if you have one.

City and parish taxes can differ. The Assessor's FAQ says the homestead exemption does not reduce city taxes, so know which bills apply to a house inside Monroe or West Monroe. A cash buyer will still run these same searches before funding, so settling them early helps any kind of sale.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I record a deed in Ouachita Parish?

Record it with the Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court, whose courthouse is on South Grand Street in Monroe. The phone number is (318) 327-1444, and filings can also go through the clerk's electronic system.

Does the Ouachita Parish Clerk of Court accept personal checks?

No. The office takes no personal checks. Online accounts and copies are paid by credit card, with a 3.49 percent convenience fee.

How much does it cost to view Ouachita Parish land records online?

The clerk charges $20 for a day, $75 for a month and $800 for a year, plus $0.50 per page. Credit cards carry a 3.49 percent fee with a $1.00 minimum.

When does the Ouachita Parish clerk's office close for holidays?

It closes on legal holidays. The 2026 closures include Thanksgiving Day, the Friday after, Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and New Year's Eve.

Where a Washington Parish deed is recorded

A Washington Parish deed is recorded with the Clerk of Court in Franklinton, who keeps the parish land records. The office is at 908-B Washington St., Franklinton, LA 70438, and the phone number is (985) 839-4663. Mail for public records requests goes to the Custodian of Records at P. O. Box 607, Franklinton, LA 70438.

Land records at this office cover mortgages, conveyances and UCC filings, along with affidavits, oaths and bonds. In Louisiana the person who passes a sale before a notary has a duty to record it. Under La. R.S. 35:199, a notary must record acts of sale of immovable property outside Orleans Parish within fifteen days with the recorder of the parish where the property sits. For a Washington Parish house, that recorder is this office.

The parish seat is Franklinton, but the property does not have to be in town. A house near Bogalusa, Angie, Varnado or Mount Hermon is recorded in the same place.

Recording fees

The posted schedule starts at $120.00 for a general recordation of 1 to 5 pages in one index type. The fee is assessed separately for each recording book, so a sale that goes into the conveyance records and a mortgage that goes into the mortgage records are charged on their own. Each tiered fee includes up to 10 names indexed and one certified copy.

That $120.00 already contains two built-in charges: a $5.00 Louisiana Clerk Remote Access Authority portal fee under La. R.S. 13:754 and a $15.00 Washington Parish Government Surcharge under La. R.S. 33:1236(55)(a). Copy prices rose to $1.00 per page on May 1, 2025.

General recordation, 1 to 5 pages$120.00

Your closing agent will add title, notary and any lender costs on top, and those are set by the people you hire, not by the parish.

Transfer tax and formatting rules

The clerk's fee schedule has no transfer tax line, only recording, indexing, certificate, cancellation, copy and similar charges. For a firm answer on your own sale, ask the clerk's land records department or your closing notary to confirm the total before closing day.

The formatting rules are the ones that cost money when missed. Every document filed for recordation must be captioned with the type of act on the first page. It needs a 2-inch top margin and 1-inch bottom and side margins on the first page, on 8 1/2 by 11 or 8 1/2 by 14 inch paper with type no smaller than 8 point. A document that misses these rules can draw the $15.00 non-compliance fee.

The clerk asks for an original and one copy. The copy is certified and returned in a self-addressed, stamped envelope that the customer supplies. In office the clerk accepts cash, check, money order or credit or debit card. By mail it takes a check or money order only.

Old liens and mortgages at a sale

Anything recorded against your house stays of record until it is cancelled, so sellers usually clear liens before or at closing. The clerk charges $55.00 for a single cancellation and $75.00 for cancelling a prescribed judgment, bond forfeiture judgment or tax lien, which includes a certificate of the clerk. A duplicate cancellation certificate is $10.00.

Judgments and liens are what sellers most often discover late. An affidavit of identity costs $23.00 for a judgment or lien dated before July 1, 2012, with no charge for one dated after that. The affidavit exists because a name on an old judgment can match a seller's name without being the same person.

A mortgage certificate is the usual way to see what is recorded against a property, at $20.00 for one name and one tract. To look yourself, the clerk offers an online records search through Cott Systems, with a 24-hour access option listed at $20.00 and a 30-day option listed at $75.00, plus $1.00 per page to print. Confirm current access prices on the login page before you pay.

  • Pull a mortgage and lien certificate in every name that has owned the house.
  • Ask for cancellations of any paid mortgage that was never released of record.
  • Check for recorded judgments in your name, and know that an affidavit of identity may be needed if the name is a common one.
  • Confirm the property description matches the deed, especially for acreage or a plat larger than 8 1/2 by 14 inches, which carries a separate $125.00 charge.

Washington Parish in brief

Washington Parish is an interior parish roughly 65 miles north of New Orleans on the Mississippi border. It was once a timber and paper hub and now has agriculture, manufacturing, food processing, retail and service businesses. The parish has 46,289 residents and 21,468 housing units, and 81.7% of those units are owner-occupied.

Bogalusa is the largest city, and International Paper still operates a paper mill and converting plant there. Louisiana Highways 10 and 21 meet in Bogalusa, and New Orleans is about an hour away via the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway. Local buyers often work at the mill, the hospitals or the other plants, which is where much of the housing demand comes from.

Assessment, appeals and inherited houses

In Louisiana the parish assessor values the property and the clerk only records the paperwork, so the two offices answer different questions. The Washington Parish Assessor's office can be reached at (985) 839-7815, and its website offers assessment search, parcel maps, exemption and re-assessment pages and forms.

To dispute a value, watch for the public inspection period. The assessment lists are open for 15 days within a 30-day window between August 15 and September 15, and the assessor publishes in the local paper which two weeks apply. A taxpayer who disagrees fills out the Notice of Appeal Request for Board of Review (form 3101) and schedules a hearing with the parish Board of Review. If either side is unhappy with the result, the Board can supply Form 3103.A for review by the Louisiana Tax Commission.

If you are selling an inherited house, the clerk's civil department handles succession, probate and tutorships, so the judgment of possession that proves your right to sell is filed with the same office that records the deed. Louisiana has not adopted transfer-on-death deeds for real property, so heirs often have to go through a succession first.

Checklist before closing

Start with the record, then the property, then the paper. Louisiana sales must be passed before a notary and then recorded in the right parish within the time the statute sets.

  • Confirm the recording parish. A parcel is recorded where it sits, not where the owner lives.
  • Order a mortgage and lien certificate and read every item on it.
  • Gather cancellation documents for paid-off loans so they can be recorded.
  • Check that the act of sale is formatted to the clerk's margin, caption and paper rules.
  • Ask whether the clerk or your notary will e-record. The clerk's online services page points to e-recording partners.
  • Look up the assessment on the assessor's search page so you know what the parish has on file.

If the house needs work, has a tenant or came through an estate, a cash buyer can close on terms that skip the repair list. We buy as-is in Washington Parish, and the recording steps above still apply to any buyer, so the clerk's fees are worth knowing either way.

Frequently asked questions

How much does the Washington Parish Clerk of Court charge to record a deed?

The posted schedule starts at $120.00 for 1 to 5 pages in one index type, $220.00 for 6 to 25 pages and $320.00 for 26 to 50 pages. Fees are assessed separately for each recording book, and each tier includes 10 indexed names and one certified copy.

Where is the Washington Parish Clerk of Court office?

It is at 908-B Washington St., Franklinton, LA 70438, phone (985) 839-4663. Public records requests are mailed to P. O. Box 607, Franklinton, LA 70438.

Does Washington Parish charge a transfer tax?

The clerk's fee schedule shows no transfer tax line. It lists recording, index, certificate, cancellation and copy charges. Ask the clerk or your closing notary to confirm the full total for your sale.

How soon must a sale be recorded in Washington Parish?

Under La. R.S. 35:199, a notary must record an act of sale of immovable property outside Orleans Parish within fifteen days with the recorder of the parish where the property is located.

Who do I call about my Washington Parish property assessment?

Call the Washington Parish Assessor at (985) 839-7815. The assessor's site also has an assessment search, maps, exemption information and the appeal forms.
